With the girls keeping a low profile and working on the side generators, there was nobody to peel Herman off on so he could catch a break. So, a hiding spot, then. Lockers were a joke. Too loud. He was moving too fast. The slam would carry down the hallway and paint a red arrow over his position. He would have to duck behind something and pray that the movement wasn’t seen before the Doctor could round a corner. He had seen Nea do it entirely too often, just dipping around something and vanishing into a bush like she had never been there. She made it look so easy — as if the Fog itself wanted her to disappear. How hard could it be? Another burst of static shot overhead — a whipcrack of voltage that sent ceiling tiles rattling in their frames. The air sparked, raw and sharp, and Jake barely had time to twist away as flecks of light burst down onto his shoulders like electric hail. He hissed between his teeth, dropped low, and dove through the nearest doorway just as the next pulse detonated behind him. The world exploded in white light. Tile cracked. Something metal shrieked against the wall. Jake didn’t look. He was already crawling. The room was tight — much smaller than he had hoped — and he slid around the edge of what looked like a drained hydrotherapy basin, ceramic walls chipped, grime-stained. It loomed just barely high enough to offer cover if he stayed low. He dropped flat beside it and pressed himself into the crook where tile met basin, chest flush to the floor, body molded tight to every possible inch of safety. And waited. His breath caught. Footsteps. Slow. Measured. Heavy enough to shake dust from the ceiling. The terror radius set his heart screaming against his ribs, Herman’s presence looming like a wall in the doorway. The sparks that danced across his gear made loud pops as they arced between muscle and the doorframe. One arc leapt sideways and lit up a rusted bar in the hallway. Jake flinched, but only internally. His jaw was locked tight. Eyes wide. Pulse screaming. Heavy breathing, tense with irritation, wafted through the room. Jake could hear every movement. The rasp of fabric, the low exhale through grit teeth, the subtle tick of a voltage regulator resetting. If the Doctor turned just a few degrees— If he spotted a boot edge, or the faint smear of dust where Jake had landed... Jake stared at the crack between basin and wall like it held the only safe geometry left in the universe . He didn’t blink. A slam shattered the stillness — a locker, not even 10 feet away. Metal on metal, loud enough to ring. Jake jerked, breath catching in his throat. The footsteps paused. Then turned. An annoyed snarl. Heavy footfalls out the far door. Silence. His heart rate slowly calmed as the radius passed down the hall. He finally allowed himself a full breath. Jake waited. Three seconds. Five. Counted them out in the gaps between heartbeats. And only then — only then — did he move. His body wasn’t moving right anymore. Twitches sparked randomly through his legs, his back, his side — all of it out of sync with anything he actually told them to do. He could feel everything, still, but it came in broken pieces. Signals half-delivered. Feedback loops without return. His heart had given up on rhythm long ago. It beat now in panicked stutters, sometimes too fast, sometimes too slow, lurching through his chest like a drunk trying to remember the steps to a song no one else could hear. His vision shimmered at the edges. A shape loomed in the doorway, blinking in and out of his vision. Massive. Looming. A silhouette writhing with violet static, jagged edges bleeding into the light. He would have flinched from it if any part of him was obeying. The light shifted, and the figure was gone. One of the Doctor’s echoes , then. Hallucinated fragments. They came more often now. He knew they weren’t real — mostly. But the body didn’t care. Especially because there was no way to tell if it was actually real until the moment passed. He counted a breath. Then another. Every breath came wrong — too shallow, too sharp. He focused on keeping the inhale relatively even, but it kept skipping. Tripping. The oxygen wasn’t landing where it was supposed to. It was making him dizzy, and relatively grateful he was already on the floor. His fingers flexed around the cuff, trying to keep a grip on the chain to ease the cut of metal into skin. The edges of the cuff were cutting deeper now. He couldn’t grip hard enough to make it matter. His shoulder was wrong . Out. He could feel it grinding with any shift of weight. He couldn’t remember when it happened. Just that it had been like this a while now — maybe minutes. Maybe hours. Time was buckling. There was a sound, distant. Footsteps. Leon turned toward it. Or — tried to . The floor didn’t move. The angle stayed the same. That wasn’t right. He tried again. Harder. The world jumped forward slightly, and he realized that he must have blacked out for a moment. Kneeling in front of him, shape fuzzed and backlit — hands on his wrist, voice low and fraying at the edges. “—got them. Leon? Hey. Hey, come on, stay with me, I got the keys—” The world didn’t click into focus so much as smear back toward it. Leon blinked, but the film stayed. His body felt... removed.
